title: Napoleon Gives Up the Pratzen Heights
text:
In late November 1805 Napoleon's army was deep in Moravia, far from France, facing a combined Russian and Austrian army under the eyes of Tsar Alexander I and Emperor Francis II. Napoleon wanted a decisive battle before more enemy forces arrived, and he set out to make the allies attack him on ground of his choosing.

He acted as if he was weak and anxious. He asked for an armistice and talks, and treated the tsar's envoy in a way that suggested he feared battle. He gave up the commanding Pratzen Heights, in the center of the battlefield, and kept his right wing, toward the south, deliberately thin, while Marshal Davout's corps was hurrying from Vienna by forced marches to reinforce it. The allied staff concluded that the French right was vulnerable and could be turned, cutting Napoleon off from Vienna.

On the morning of 2 December 1805 the allies did exactly that. Column after column marched down from the Pratzen Heights to attack the French right, where Davout's arriving troops held them. As the heights emptied, Marshal Soult's corps, hidden in the fog in the valley below, climbed the slope and seized them as the sun broke through. The allied army was cut in two, and its southern wing was trapped and driven back against frozen ponds.

Austria made peace within weeks, and the Russians withdrew. Austerlitz became Napoleon's most celebrated victory.
lesson: Showing weakness at the right point can invite an opponent into the move you have prepared for. Make the attractive option the one that serves you.
people: Napoleon Bonaparte, Louis-Nicolas Davout, Jean-de-Dieu Soult, Alexander I, Mikhail Kutuzov
location: Austerlitz (modern Slavkov u Brna, Czech Republic)
source: Napoleon's 30th Bulletin of the Grande Armee (1805); David Chandler, The Campaigns of Napoleon (1966)
place: Pratzen Heights, near Slavkov u Brna, Czech Republic
